# Differentiable and inverse volume rendering
Also called: Inverse volume rendering, Differentiable rendering for volumes
## Overview
This family encompasses methods that treat volume rendering as a differentiable operation to solve inverse problems, optimizing 3D scene representations from 2D observations without requiring 3D ground truth supervision [S2, unofficial][S3, unofficial]. It sets itself apart from standard rasterization or path tracing by enabling end-to-end optimization of [implicit fields](#13-procedural-and-implicit-volumes.md), explicit grids, and physical parameters via gradient descent [S5, unofficial]. It differs from [Radiance-field optimization](44-radiance-field-optimization.md) by focusing on the general differentiability of the volume rendering integral rather than specific neural field architectures, and from [Tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering](45-tomographic-reconstruction-as-inverse-rendering.md) by encompassing both tomographic and non-tomographic (e.g., RGB-only) optimization loops [S5, unofficial].
## Shared principles
All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the [forward rendering](#1816-per-voxel-projection-object-order.md) operator and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps. The core mechanism is the evaluation of the [volume rendering equation](#2098-volume-rendering-equation.md) and the computation of gradients with respect to scene parameters (density, geometry, transfer functions, camera poses).

The standard [emission-absorption model](#927-emission-absorption-model.md) computes the color $\hat{C}(\mathbf{r})$ for a ray $\mathbf{r}$ as [S1][S5, unofficial]:

$$
\hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{i=1}^N T_i (1 - \exp(-\sigma_i \delta_i)) \mathbf{c}_i
$$

where $\sigma_i$ is the density, $\delta_i$ is the step size, $\mathbf{c}_i$ is the color, and $T_i = \exp\left(-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma_j \delta_j\right)$ is the transmittance [S1][S5, unofficial].

Differentiation strategies fall into three main categories:
1.  **Reverse-Mode Automatic Differentiation (AD):** Standard backpropagation through the computational graph. This requires storing $O(kn)$ intermediate states (where $n$ is pixels and $k$ is samples), leading to high memory usage [S5, unofficial].
2.  **[Adjoint Method](#789-adjoint-method.md):** Computes gradients by propagating adjoint variables backward through the rendering algorithm, evaluating the chain rule from output to input. This has computational complexity largely constant in the number of parameters, making it preferable for optimizing many parameters like the transfer function [S1][S3, unofficial].
3.  **Analytic Inversion / Explicit Gradients:** Uses a-priori knowledge of the DVR operations to invert the order of operations or derive closed-form gradients, reducing memory consumption to $O(n)$ by avoiding the storage of intermediate results [S5, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Differentiable volume rendering](43-differentiable-volume-rendering.md)
[Differentiable volume rendering](#43-differentiable-volume-rendering.md) computes the gradient of a rendered image (or derived metric like depth) with respect to scene parameters by making the rendering integral differentiable. It solves the inverse problem of optimizing 3D scene representations from 2D observations without requiring 3D ground truth supervision. Unlike standard rasterization or path tracing which may lack analytical gradients for complex volumetric interactions, this family enables end-to-end optimization of implicit fields, explicit grids, and physical parameters via gradient descent. It sets itself apart from [Radiance-field optimization](44-radiance-field-optimization.md) by focusing on the general differentiability of the volume rendering integral itself, rather than specific neural field architectures, and from [Tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering](45-tomographic-reconstruction-as-inverse-rendering.md) by encompassing both tomographic and non-tomographic (e.g., RGB-only) optimization loops.

### [Radiance-field optimization](44-radiance-field-optimization.md)
[Radiance-field optimization](#44-radiance-field-optimization.md) is the process of reconstructing a 3D scene representation (a "radiance field") from a set of 2D images by minimizing the photometric error between rendered views and ground-truth observations. It solves the inverse problem of determining the underlying volumetric or implicit scene properties (density, color, geometry) that produced the input images. What sets it apart from explicit grid-based siblings like [Explicit Radiance Fields](806-explicit-radiance-fields.md) and [Plenoxels](1501-plenoxels.md) is the frequent use of neural networks (typically MLPs) or factorized tensor structures to represent the scene implicitly, allowing for high-fidelity reconstruction of complex geometry and view-dependent appearance without explicit mesh or voxel structures. It builds on [Differentiable and inverse volume rendering](42-differentiable-and-inverse-volume-rendering.md) by treating the scene parameters as differentiable variables updated via gradient descent.

### [Tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering](45-tomographic-reconstruction-as-inverse-rendering.md)
[Tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering](#45-tomographic-reconstruction-as-inverse-rendering.md) treats computed tomography (CT) not as a linear algebra problem to be solved via closed-form filters or static iterative solvers, but as an optimization problem where a differentiable forward renderer (the projector) is minimized against measured projection data. This approach unifies classical algebraic reconstruction techniques (ART, [SIRT](#3101-sirt-simultaneous-iterative-reconstruction-technique.md)) with modern [neural representations](#10-neural-and-primitive-based-representations.md) and compressive sensing priors under a single gradient-based framework. It distinguishes itself from [Differentiable volume rendering](43-differentiable-and-inverse-volume-rendering.md) by focusing specifically on the tomographic geometry (parallel/fan/cone beam) and the reconstruction of density/absorption fields from sparse or noisy sinograms, and from [Radiance-field optimization](44-radiance-field-optimization.md) by explicitly modeling the X-ray physics (Beer-Lambert law) rather than just RGB appearance.

## Background
The integration of differentiability into volume rendering emerged from the need to optimize 3D structures from 2D data without explicit 3D supervision. Early work focused on analytic gradients for differentiable volume rendering [S5, unofficial], while later developments unified tomographic reconstruction with inverse rendering techniques [S1, unofficial][S2]. The field has evolved to support both neural implicit representations and explicit grid-based optimizations, driven by applications in novel view synthesis and medical imaging.
